readings.c2s1:
¶
'''unvascular''' (un-vas′kụ̄-lär), ''a.'' Non-vascular; containing no blood-vessels.

'''unvassal''' (un-vas′al), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''vassal.''] To cause to be no longer a vassal; release from vassalage. [Rare.]

'''unveil''' (un-vāl′), ''v.'' [Early mod. E. ''unvail;'' < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''veil.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To remove a veil from; uncover; disclose to view; reveal: as, to ''unveil'' a statue. ''Shak.'', T. and C., iii. 3. 200.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become unveiled; be disclosed to view; remove a veil; reveal one’s self.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unveil'', O Lord, and on us shine
In glory and in grace.</poem>
{{right|''J. H. Newman'', The Two Worlds.}}}}
Also ''unvail.''

'''unveiledly''' (un-vā′led-li), ''adv.'' Plainly; without disguise. ''Boyle'', Works, IV. 18. [Rare.]

'''unveiler''' (un-vā′lėr), ''n.'' One who unveils; hence, one who expounds. ''Boyle'', Works, IV. 18.

'''unvenerable''' (un-ven′e̤-ra̤-bl), ''a.'' Not venerable; not worthy of veneration; contemptible. ''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 3. 77.

'''unvenomed''' (un-ven′umd), ''a.'' Having no venom; not poisonous: as, a toad ''unvenomed.'' ''Bp. Hall'', Satires, Postscript.

'''unvenomous''' (un-ven′um-us), ''a.'' Same as ''unvenomed.'' ''Bp. Gauden'', Tears of the Church, p. 297. (''Davies.'')

'''unvented''' (un-ven′ted), ''a.'' Not vented; not
readings.c2s2:
'''unventilated''' (un-ven′ti-lā-ted), ''a.'' Not ventilated. ''Sir R. Blackmore.''

'''unveracious''' (un-vē-rā′shus), ''a.'' Not veracious; not having a strict regard for truth; untruthful; dishonest; false.

'''unveracity''' (un-vē-ras′i̤-ti), ''n.'' Want of veracity; untruth; falsehood.
{{smaller block|A certain very considerable finite quantity of ''Unveracity'' and Phantasm.{{right|''Carlyle.''}}}}

'''unverdant''' (un-vėr′da̤nt), ''a.'' Not verdant; not green; having no verdure. ''Congreve'', tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love, iii.

'''unveritable†''' (un-ver′i-ta-bl), ''a.'' Not veritable; not true. ''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 21.

'''unversed''' (un-vėrst′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not skilled; not versed; unacquainted.
{{smaller block|A mind in all heart-mysteries ''unversed.''{{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion, vi.}}}}
'''2.''' Not put in verse: as, thoughts ''unversed.''

'''unvessel†''' (un-ves′el), ''v. t.'' To empty. [Rare.]

'''unvexed''' (un-vekst′), ''a.'' Not vexed; not troubled; not disturbed; not agitated or disquieted. ''Donne'', Anatomy of the World, i. Also ''unvext.''
{{smaller block|<poem>In the noon now woodland creatures all
Were resting ’neath the shadow of the trees,
Patient, ''unvexed'' by any memories.</poem>{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 174.}}}}

'''unvicar''' (un-vik′ä̤r), ''v. t.'' To deprive of the office or position of vicar.
{{smaller block|If I had your authority, I would be so bold to ''unvicar'' him.{{right|''Strype'', Cranmer, II. vii. (''Davies.'')}}}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unviolable''' (un-vī′ọ-la-bl), ''a.'' Not to be violated or broken. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 1. 27. [Rare.]

'''unviolated''' (un-vī′ọ-lā-ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not violated; not injured.
{{smaller block|Th’ ''unviolated'' honour of your wife.
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iii. 1. 88.}}}}
'''2.''' Not broken; not transgressed: as, an ''unviolated'' vow. ''Milton'', S. A., l. 1144.

'''unvirtue''' (un-vėr′t̮ū), ''n.'' Absence of virtue; vice. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They think their children never do unvirtuous things; and yet they reek with ''unvirtue.''
{{right|''H. W. Beecher'', Christian Union, March 3, 1887.}}}}

'''unvirtuous''' (un-vėr′t̮ū-us), ''a.'' Not virtuous; destitute of virtue. ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iv. 2. 232.

'''unvirtuously''' (un-vėr′t̮ū-us-li), ''adv.'' In an unvirtuous manner; viciously.

'''unvisible†''' (un-viz′i-bl), ''a.'' Invisible. ''Chaucer.''

'''unvisibly†''' (un-viz′i-bli), ''adv.'' Invisibly. ''Bp. Gardiner.''

'''unvital''' (un-vī′tal), ''a.'' Not vital; not essential to life; hence, fatal. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Lavoisier showed that the atmospheric air consists of pure or vital, and of an ''unvital'' air, which he thence called azote.
{{right|''Whewell.''}}}}

'''unvitiated''' (un-vish′i-ā-ted), ''a.'' Not vitiated; not corrupted; pure. ''B. Jonson.'' Magnetick Lady, iv. 3.

'''unvizard''' (un-viz′ärd), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''vizard.''] To divest of a vizard or mask; unmask.
{{smaller block|O what a death it is to the Prelates to be thus ''un-visarded'', thus uncas’d.
{{right|''Milton'', On Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''unvoiced''' (un-voist′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not spoken; unuttered; not articulated or pronounced. ''Emerson.''—'''2.''' In ''phonetics'', not uttered with voice as distinct from breath; unintonated; surd.

'''unvoidable''' (un-voi′da̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being made void; irreversible.
{{smaller block|He will from on high pronounce that ''unvoidable'' sentence.
{{right|''Bailey'', tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, p. 173. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unvoluntary†''' (un-vol′un-tạ̄-ri), ''a.'' Involuntary. ''Fuller.''

'''unvoluptuous''' (un-vọ̄-lup′tụ̄-us), ''a.'' Free from voluptuousness; not sensuous. ''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, xxiii.

'''unvote''' (un-vōt′), ''v. t.'' To retract, annul, or undo by vote.
{{smaller block|This was so sacred a rule that many of those who voted with the court the day before, expressed their indignation against it, as subverting the very constitution of parliament, if things might be thus voted and ''unvoted'' again from day to day. ''Bp. Burnet'', Hist. Own Times, an. 1711.}}

'''unvowed''' (un-voud′), ''a.'' Not vowed; not consecrated by solemn promise.
{{smaller block|If ''vnuowed'' to another Order, . . . he vows in this order.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 229. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unvoyageable''' (un-voi′ạ̄j-a̤-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Incapable of being navigated; innavigable. ''De Quincey.''—'''2.''' Not to be crossed or passed over; impassable.
{{smaller block|<poem>This ''unvoyageable'' gulf obscure.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 366.}}}}

'''unvulgar''' (un-vul′gä̤r), ''a.'' Not vulgar or common.
readings.c3s2:
{{smaller block|<poem>Heat my brain
With Delphic fire,
That I may sing my thoughts in some ''unvulgar'' strain.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Underwoods, xliv.}}}}

'''unvulgarize''' (un-vul′gär-īz), ''v. t.'' To divest of vulgarity; make not vulgar or common. ''Lamb.''

'''unwaited''' (un-wā′ted), ''a.'' Not attended: with ''on''.
{{smaller block|To wander up and down ''unwaited on.''
{{right|''Fletcher'', Mad Lover, ii.}}}}

'''unwakeful''' (un-wāk′fu̇l), ''a.'' Sleeping easily and soundly; characterized by sound sleep.

'''unwakefulness''' (un-wāk′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unwakeful; sound sleep.

'''unwakened''' (un-wā′knd), ''a.'' Not wakened; not roused from sleep or as from sleep. ''Milton'', P. L., v. 9.

'''unwallet''' (un-wol′et), ''v. t.'' To take from a wallet.
{{smaller block|The lacquey laughed, unsheathed his calabash, and ''unwalleted'' his cheese.
{{right|''Jarvis'', tr. of Don Quixote, II. iv. 14. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unwandering''' (un-won′dėr-ing), ''a.'' Not wandering; not moving or going from place to place. ''Cowper'', Iliad, xiii.

'''unwappered†''' (un-wop′ėrd), ''a.'' Not caused or not having reason to tremble; not made tremulous; unpalsied; hence, fearless and strong through innocence.
{{smaller block|<poem>We come towards the gods,
Young and ''unwapper’d'', not halting under crimes
Many and stale.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Two Noble Kinsmen, v. 4.}}}}

'''unwarded†''' (un-wâr′ded), ''a.'' Unwatched; unguarded. ''J. Brende'', tr. of Quintus Curtius,
readings.c3s3:
fol. 81.

'''unware†''' (un-wãr′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unwar'', ''onwar'', < AS. ''unwær'', unheeding, unheeded, unexpected, < ''un-'', not, + ''wær'', heedful: see ''un-''<sup>1</sup> and ''ware''<sup>1</sup>.] Unexpected; unforeseen.
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon thy glade day have in thy mynde
The ''unwar'' wo or harm that comth bihynde.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law’s Tale, l. 329.}}}}

'''unware†''' (un-wãr′), ''adv.'' [ME. ''unwar''; prop. predicate use of ''unware'', ''a.''] Unawares; unexpectedly.
{{smaller block|<poem>On thee, Fortune, I pleyne,
That ''unwar'' wrapped hast me in thy cheyne.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Franklin’s Tale, l. 628.}}
He put vp his goode swerde for doute leste he slough eny man ''vn-war''.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 493.}}}}

'''unwarely†''' (un-wãr′li), ''adv.'' [< ''unwarely'', ''unwarly'', ''unwarliche'', < AS. ''unwærlīce'', unexpectedly, < ''unwær'', unexpected: see ''unware'', ''a.''] Unawares; unforeseen; unexpectedly.
{{smaller block|Elde is comen ''unwarly'' upon me.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. meter 1.}}}}

'''unwareness†''' (un-wãr′nes), ''n.'' [< ''unware'' + ''-ness''.] The condition of being unexpected. ''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 201.

'''unwares†''' (un-wãrz′), ''adv.'' [< ME. *''unwares'', < AS. ''unwæres'', < ''unwær'', unexpected: see ''unware''.] Unawares; by surprise.
{{smaller block|A great sort of Turks entred into the bulwarke of Spaine, . . . and droue our men out, I can not tell how, ''vnwares'' or otherwise.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. 84.}}}}

'''unwakeful''' (un-wāk′fu̇l), ''a.'' Sleeping easily and soundly; characterized by sound sleep.

'''unwakefulness''' (un-wāk′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unwakeful; sound sleep.

'''unwakened''' (un-wā′knd), ''a.'' Not wakened; not roused from sleep or as from sleep. ''Milton'', P. L., v. 9.

'''unwallet''' (un-wol′et), ''v. t.'' To take from a wallet.
{{smaller block|The lacquey laughed, unsheathed his calabash, and ''unwalleted'' his cheese.
{{right|''Jarvis'', tr. of Don Quixote, II. iv. 14. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unwandering''' (un-won′dėr-ing), ''a.'' Not wandering; not moving or going from place to place. ''Cowper'', Iliad, xiii.

'''unwappered†''' (un-wop′ėrd), ''a.'' Not caused or not having reason to tremble; not made tremulous; unpalsied; hence, fearless and strong through innocence.
{{smaller block|<poem>We come towards the gods,
Young and ''unwapper’d'', not halting under crimes
Many and stale.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Two Noble Kinsmen, v. 4.}}}}

'''unwarded†''' (un-wâr′ded), ''a.'' Unwatched; unguarded. ''J. Brende'', tr. of Quintus Curtius, fol. 81.

'''unware†''' (un-wãr′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unwar'', ''onwar'', < AS. ''unwær'', unheeding, unheeded, unexpected, < ''un-'', not, + ''wær'', heedful: see ''un-''<sup>1</sup> and ''ware''<sup>1</sup>.] Unexpected; unforeseen.
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon thy glade day have in thy mynde
The ''unwar'' wo or harm that comth bihynde.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law’s Tale, l. 329.}}}}

'''unware†''' (un-wãr′), ''adv.'' [ME. ''unwar''; prop. predicate use of ''unware'', ''a.''] Unawares; unexpectedly.
{{smaller block|<poem>On thee, Fortune, I pleyne,
That ''unwar'' wrapped hast me in thy cheyne.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Franklin’s Tale, l. 628.}}
He put vp his goode swerde for doute leste he slough eny man ''vn-war''.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 493.}}}}

'''unwarely†''' (un-wãr′li), ''adv.'' [< ''unwarely'', ''unwarly'', ''unwarliche'', < AS. ''unwærlīce'', unexpectedly, < ''unwær'', unexpected: see ''unware'', ''a.''] Unawares; unforeseen; unexpectedly.
{{smaller block|Elde is comen ''unwarly'' upon me.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. meter 1.}}}}

'''unwareness†''' (un-wãr′nes), ''n.'' [< ''unware'' + ''-ness''.] The condition of being unexpected. ''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 201.

'''unwares†''' (un-wãrz′), ''adv.'' [< ME. *''unwares'', < AS. ''unwæres'', < ''unwær'', unexpected: see ''unware''.] Unawares; by surprise.
{{smaller block|A great sort of Turks entred into the bulwarke of Spaine, . . . and droue our men out, I can not tell how, ''vnwares'' or otherwise.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. 84.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
